# Ajakalāpaka Sutta (Ud 1.7 (PTS Ud 4))

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Ajakalāpaka Sutta* (Ud 1.7, PTS Ud 4) is the seventh discourse of the first chapter (Bodhivagga) of the *Udāna* [SuttaCentral]. Set at the Ajakalāpaka Shrine in Pāvā, the narrative recounts an episode where the Buddha is seated out in the open air during a dark night while light rain is falling [Masefield 1997]. Intending to provoke fear, stupefaction, and horripilation in the Buddha, the resident *yakkha* Ajakalāpaka approaches him, eliciting an inspired utterance in which the Buddha declares that an awakened person who has penetrated the truth and eradicated defilements has gone beyond all fear [SuttaCentral; Masefield 1997].

The sutta and its titular spirit-deity are cited in scholarly studies of early Buddhist popular religion and iconography; Robert DeCaroli discusses Ajakalāpaka as an example of a local spirit associated with a specific shrine who also finds mention in monument inscriptions such as those at Bhārhut [DeCaroli 2004], and Étienne Lamotte examined the figure in a dedicated comparative study of the *yakṣas* Ajakalāpaka and Bakkula [Lamotte 1987].

SuttaCentral notes verse parallels in the Sanskrit and Tibetan *Udānavarga* (UV 33, UVS 33, Uv Kg 33) and the Chinese *Udānavarga* translations (*Chuyao jing*, T 212.34, and *Faji yaosong jing*, T 213.33), along with a reference in the *Nettippakaraṇa* (Ne 37) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus identifies substantial Pali-internal text reuse of stock prose formulations describing demonic intimidation and nocturnal meditation, particularly with the *Māra Saṁyutta* (SN 4), *Bhikkhunī Saṁyutta* (SN 5), the Vinaya *Mahākhandhaka* (Kd 1), *Brahma Saṁyutta* (SN 6), and neighboring discourses of the *Udāna* (Ud 1.1 and Ud 1.2) [DharmaNexus].
